title: The profitability framework for case interviews
description: "How can the client make more profit?" Profits are falling, or the client wants them higher. The structure, the first question to ask, and practice prompts wi
hook: Profit questions are the most common cases of all, so this is the framework worth knowing best. The idea is simple: profit is revenue minus costs, so you find out which side moved and why. Here is how to lay it out, the first question to ask, and how to make it fit the client in front of you.
body:
When you will use it

Profits are falling, or the client wants them higher.

This is a diagnose question: "Why is this happening, and how do we fix it?" Break the problem into parts that add up, find which part moved, then fix that part. More on the three families of case questions.

Ask this first

Is it revenue, costs or both? Is the whole industry hit, or just us?

One good question at the start can halve the work. It tells you where to look, and it shows the interviewer you are thinking about the client, not reciting a list.

The structure

  • Revenue (revenue = units × price)
    • Units sold (customers × purchases each)
    • Price per unit
  • Costs
    • Fixed costs (rent · salaried staff · overheads)
    • Variable costs (materials · delivery · commissions)

Say it out loud as a short sentence per branch, then say which branch you would look at first and why. That last part, your hypothesis, is what most candidates forget.

Make it your own

Split every line by product, customer segment and channel: a shift in mix often hides inside the averages. Compare each line with competitors to tell a company problem from a market problem.

Interviewers can tell when a structure has been memorised. Swap the general words for words about this client: not "costs", but "fuel and crew costs" for an airline.

Practise with real prompts

Read each prompt, take two minutes to sketch your own structure, then compare.

1. A national bank's mortgage applications are down 20% this year. Why?

Show a model structure
  • Market: Total applications in the market: rates, house prices, transactions; Is everyone down 20%, or just us?
  • Our offer: Rates and fees vs rivals; Loan-to-value limits, product range
  • Channels: Brokers: are they placing less with us?; Online and branch: traffic, conversion
  • Process: Time to decision, approval rate (brokers avoid slow or strict lenders); Drop-off during the application

Where to start: The market first: if all banks are down 20%, it is not our problem to fix.

The trap: Jumping to marketing ideas before checking whether the whole market fell.

2. A ski resort's profits fell 40% after two warm winters.

Show a model structure
  • Winter revenue: Visitors × spend, by month; Lift passes, ski school, food, rentals
  • Costs: Fixed costs: lifts, staff, maintenance; Variable and snow-related: snowmaking, energy
  • Snow risk: Days open, altitude, snowmaking coverage; Trend or two bad years? Share of revenue pre-sold as season passes
  • Non-ski income: Summer, events, conferences; Year-round use of lifts, hotels and restaurants

Where to start: Days open: warm winters cut the season, and costs are mostly fixed.

The trap: Treating it as a normal profit decline and missing that weather is the root cause.

3. A cinema chain's attendance is still 25% below pre-pandemic levels.

Show a model structure
  • Market: Total cinema attendance vs ours; Film supply: fewer big releases?
  • Our offer: Ticket and snack prices; Comfort, screens, locations
  • Substitutes: Streaming windows shorter; Home viewing habits
  • Customers: Which groups have not come back; Frequency vs number of visitors

Where to start: Market vs us: are we below the industry, or is the whole market smaller?

The trap: Ignoring the supply of films, which drives most of the attendance.
outro: Read it once, then try it on a practice case today while it is fresh. One real attempt teaches more than three re-reads. You can see this tree drawn step by step, and every other core framework, on the free frameworks page.
